subject: Behavioral Economics
title: Scaling Nudges Globally
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Scaling Nudges Globally.

hook.text: A hand-washing nudge in Bangladesh cut diarrhea by 36%. Painted footprints led children to sinks. No lectures.

buildup.text: The World Bank and UN now fund behavioral units in developing countries. Low-cost nudges can tackle problems.

discovery.text: Nudges are cheap to implement. A text reminder about a doctor's appointment reduces no-shows by 25%.

twist.text: Nudges that work in one culture may fail in another. Social-norm messages fail where conformity is low.

climax.text: Behavioral interventions must be tested locally before global rollout. The principle is universal but the details.

punchline.text: The cheapest intervention is the one that matches the culture.

quiz.question: Why must nudges be tested locally before scaling globally?
options: Nudges are too expensive to implement widely
What works in one culture may fail in another due to different norms
Nudges only work in wealthy countries

details.summary: Scaling nudges globally requires adapting interventions to diverse cultural, institutional, and economic contexts. What works in Western democracies may fail in different cultural settings, and the infrastructure for implementation varies dramatically across countries.
details.whyItMatters: Over 200 nudge units now operate globally, but most evidence comes from wealthy Western countries. Scaling behavioral policy to developing nations and different cultural contexts requires understanding how culture shapes the effectiveness of nudges.
takeaways: Nudge effectiveness varies significantly across cultural contexts
Social norm nudges can backfire in cultures with different reference groups
Implementation infrastructure limits scalability in developing countries

faq.question: Why might nudges that work in one country fail in another?
faq.answer: Cultural differences in trust, social norms, individualism, and government legitimacy all affect how people respond. Social proof nudges depend on who the reference group is. Default effects depend on trust in the default-setter.

faq.question: How many nudge units exist globally?
faq.answer: Over 200 as of recent counts, operating across every continent. The UK Behavioural Insights Team was the first, followed by units in the US, Singapore, Australia, and many others. The concept has spread faster than almost any policy innovation.
